surfaced_article.title: Twenty Years Later: The Lasting Lessons of Enron

relevance_explanation:
Reading the Enron article now would feel different because the new article has established that access to information was never the true source of expertise — judgment, question-framing, and the ability to interrogate what you already know are — which changes what the Enron article means.

The Powers Report's damning finding about Enron's board was not that they lacked information: they were briefed, they received reports, they approved transactions. The failure was that they had "inability to appreciate the significance of information provided" and conducted only "cursory" reviews — they couldn't ask the right probing questions of the data in front of them. The article frames this as a governance breakdown, but through the lens of the new piece, it reads as a catastrophic failure of exactly the three meta-expertise capabilities the new article identifies: creative synthesis across domains (connecting the dots between SPE structures), contextual wisdom to recognize red flags as significant, and ethical navigation of competing interests when insiders had conflicts.

The non-obvious reprise: the new article argues that AI is now stripping away the illusion that information-holders are the valuable people in an organization. Enron's board collapse is a pre-AI case study proving that illusion was always dangerous — experienced, prominent directors were exposed as holding credentials without meta-expertise, with catastrophic results. The new article's warning about "cognitive atrophy" from outsourcing thinking maps directly onto what the Powers Report describes as a board that had outsourced its judgment to management. Enron becomes not just a governance story but a founding exhibit for why judgment and question-framing — not information access — must be the real bar for senior expertise.
